title: Gödel's Completeness Theorem and What 'Sound' and 'Complete' Actually Mean (1929-1930)
explainer: Kurt Gödel's 1929 dissertation proved that first-order logic is complete: every statement true in all models has a formal proof. That result is the historical source of the vocabulary, soundness (every provable statement is true) and completeness (every true statement is provable), that type-system and program-analysis papers use constantly. Knowing where those words come from makes it far easier to read a paper's claim that a system is 'sound but not complete' as a precise, checkable statement rather than a vague compliment.

title: Ronald Fisher and the 0.05 Threshold Behind Every Benchmark Claim (1925)
explainer: The p-value and the 0.05 'significance' cutoff that AI and systems papers use to argue one model or technique beats another trace to Ronald Fisher's 1925 book 'Statistical Methods for Research Workers,' where he offered 0.05 as a convenient guideline, not a law of nature. Reading a results table's statistical claims critically means knowing that this threshold is a historical convention Fisher himself did not intend to be fixed, later formalized further by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson. That context is exactly what separates a credulous read of 'statistically significant' from a literate one.
